h: Marble Halls and a Viceroy's Treasures
p: The Curzon family have been at Kedleston since the twelfth century, which is a remarkable run by anyone's standards. The most famous of them, George Nathaniel Curzon, served as Viceroy of India at the turn of the twentieth century. By coincidence, Government House in Calcutta had been modelled on Kedleston long before he arrived, so he found himself living in a version of his own family home thousands of miles away.

Curzon brought back a large collection of objects from his travels in Asia, and these are displayed in the Eastern Museum inside the house. The pieces open a window on a complicated chapter of empire, and they're thought-provoking as well as beautiful.

When you step into the Marble Hall, look up and around at the towering columns of pink-veined Derbyshire alabaster. It's a jaw-dropper of a room, designed to give visitors a sense of arriving in an ancient Roman temple.
Allow at least half a day. Out in the park, look for Robert Adam's bridge and fishing room by the lakes, both lovely spots for a pause.

Derby has plenty to add on. Derby Museum and Art Gallery holds a major collection of paintings by Joseph Wright of Derby, and the Museum of Making in the old Silk Mill tells the city's industrial story. The Derwent Valley Mills, a World Heritage Site that stretches north from Derby, are a fascinating extra for history lovers.
